lesson.text: Quick memory: what are complementary colours? (Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel, like blue and orange.) Today: what art is made of, and how artists arrange it.
The elements are the building blocks of art: line, shape, form (a 3D shape), colour, tone (light and dark), texture and space.

The principles are how artists arrange the elements. Balance makes a picture feel steady: symmetrical balance mirrors both halves, and asymmetrical balance weighs one big shape against several small ones.
Radial balance spreads out from the middle, like a flower, a wheel or a round cathedral window.
Contrast puts opposites side by side: light and dark, big and small, rough and smooth. Emphasis makes one part stand out, the focal point, where your eye lands first.
Rhythm repeats shapes or colours with a regular beat, like music. Movement leads your eye along a path. Pattern repeats one motif in rows.
Unity makes everything belong together, like shapes sharing one family of colours. Variety adds differences so it is not dull. Good art balances the two.
Try it in the world: build a wall in your world with symmetry, a focal point and a rhythm of blocks. Ask a friend which principles they can spot. Next: world art from 500 to 1500.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.hint: Is one half a mirror of the other?
exercises.explain: It shows symmetrical balance: the two halves mirror each other.

exercises.prompt: Match each element to what it means.
matches: a mark made by a moving point
exercises.hint: Think about drawing, shading and touching.
exercises.explain: Line is a moving point's mark, tone is light and dark, texture is how it feels, and form is a 3D shape.

exercises.prompt: The focal point is the part your eye goes to first.
exercises.hint: Think of the one orange circle among grey ones.
exercises.explain: True: emphasis makes a focal point that catches your eye first.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.explain: It shows emphasis: one big red circle stands out as the focal point.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: an element of art, or a principle?
exercises.hint: Elements are what art is made of; principles are how it is arranged.
exercises.explain: Elements: line, colour, texture. Principles: balance, contrast, rhythm.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.hint: It feels steady, but the two sides are not mirrors.
exercises.explain: It shows asymmetrical balance: one big square is balanced by several small circles.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.explain: It shows radial balance: everything spreads out from the middle.

exercises.prompt: How can an artist make one shape the focal point?
exercises.hint: What makes the orange circle stand out?
choices: make it differ in colour or size from the rest
make it the same as everything else
exercises.explain: A shape that differs from the rest, by colour or size, catches the eye.

exercises.prompt: Asymmetrical balance means the picture looks unbalanced.
exercises.hint: Think of the seesaw with one big weight.
exercises.explain: False: it is still balanced, just not mirrored: one big shape weighs as much as several small ones.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.hint: Big, small, big, small: like a beat.
exercises.explain: It shows rhythm: shapes repeat with a regular beat, big and small.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.hint: Different shapes, but do they belong together?
exercises.explain: It shows unity: different shapes share one family of blues.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.explain: It shows variety: every shape, colour and size is different.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design show most?
exercises.explain: It shows movement: the curve leads your eye across, with the circles growing.

exercises.prompt: A painting has one big dark tree on the left and three small birds on the right, and it feels steady. Which principle is that?
exercises.hint: The sides are not the same, but it feels steady.
exercises.explain: One big shape balances several small ones: asymmetrical balance.

exercises.prompt: Too much unity can make a picture dull, so artists add some variety.
exercises.hint: Imagine a whole picture of the same grey square.
exercises.explain: True: a little variety keeps unity interesting.

exercises.prompt: Sort these by their kind of balance.
items: a big rock and three pebbles
a face seen from the front
a tree on one side, birds on the other
exercises.hint: Mirror halves, spreading from a middle, or different but steady?
exercises.explain: Symmetry: wings, a face. Radial: a wheel, a sunflower. Asymmetry: a rock and pebbles, a tree and birds.

exercises.prompt: Match each principle to what it does.
exercises.hint: Emphasis gives a picture its focal point.
exercises.explain: Contrast puts opposites side by side, emphasis makes one part stand out, and unity makes everything belong together.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: does it add unity or variety?
items: shapes in one family of colours
a mix of curves and corners
exercises.hint: Unity makes things belong together; variety adds differences.
exercises.explain: Unity: one family of colours, a repeated line, matching textures. Variety: different sizes, a surprise colour, a mix of curves and corners.

exercises.prompt: Match each artwork to the principle it uses most.
items: one red boat in a grey sea
a path that leads into the hills
exercises.hint: Does it spread from a middle, repeat a motif, stand out, or lead your eye?
exercises.explain: A round window spreads out from its middle: radial balance. Repeating tiles: pattern. One red boat stands out in the grey: emphasis. A path leads your eye into the hills: movement.
